descriptions:
Clinical Neurology develops the structured reasoning that distinguishes confident neurological practice: the disciplined progression from history and examination to anatomical localisation and a prioritised differential diagnosis. The course is built around the bedside and revisits the neurological examination not as a checklist but as a hypothesis-driven investigation.

The curriculum then works through the disorders a neurologist meets most often — headache, epilepsy, movement disorders and the neurodegenerative diseases — emphasising pattern recognition, appropriate investigation and current principles of management. A closing block of integrated case discussions consolidates the method, asking the learner to localise, differentiate and plan as they would in clinic.

The course is intended for neurology residents, medical students and clinicians seeking a systematic foundation in clinical neurological decision-making.

Neuroscience provides the mechanistic foundation on which clinical neurology rests. Beginning at the level of the single neuron, the course establishes the cellular and electrical principles of neural signalling before advancing to synaptic transmission and the neurotransmitter systems that are the targets of much of modern therapeutics.

Later modules move from cell to circuit, examining neuroplasticity, the organisation of neural networks, and the cognitive systems — attention, memory, language and executive function — that emerge from them. Each concept is linked to its clinical correlate so that mechanism continually informs practice.

The course suits students and clinicians who want a rigorous, concept-led grounding in cellular and systems neuroscience.

Neuroimaging teaches a systematic, transferable approach to interpreting the studies that now underpin almost every neurological decision. The course begins with the physical principles of CT and MRI, to the depth a clinician requires, then builds disciplined search patterns for reading the head CT and the core MRI sequences.

Dedicated modules address the techniques that most often determine management — diffusion imaging in acute stroke, CT and MR angiography in vascular disease, and the principles of functional imaging — before a concluding case-based review. Throughout, emphasis falls on recognising critical findings and avoiding common interpretive pitfalls.

It is designed for trainees in neurology, emergency medicine and radiology who wish to read studies with confidence.

Brain Anatomy presents functional neuroanatomy as the working language of clinical neurology, with every structure tied to its function and to the deficit produced when it fails. The course is organised regionally, progressing from the cerebral lobes through the brainstem, diencephalon, basal ganglia and cerebellum.

A final block traces the major white-matter pathways that connect these regions into functional systems, and a clinical review relates the anatomy directly to examination findings and lesion localisation.

The detailed, region-by-region structure makes the course suitable both as a first systematic course in neuroanatomy and as a focused revision resource ahead of postgraduate examinations.

Neurocritical Care addresses the management of patients with life-threatening neurological illness, where decisions are made in minutes and physiological monitoring guides every intervention. The course opens with the organisation of the neurocritical care unit and the principles of multimodal neuromonitoring.

Subsequent modules cover the conditions that define the specialty — raised intracranial pressure, acute stroke, status epilepticus, and traumatic and hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury — each presented with current, protocol-driven management. A concluding module on neurocritical decision-making, including prognostication, draws the threads together.

The course is aimed at neurology and intensive-care trainees and the wider neuro-ICU team.

Neurosurgery introduces the principles, anatomy and core procedures of the specialty for surgical trainees and for the clinicians who work alongside the operating team. The early modules establish safe operative practice and the surgical anatomy of the corridors through which the brain and spine are approached.

The course then covers the cranial approaches, image-guided navigation and intra-operative monitoring that define modern surgery, before surveying the major subspecialties: tumour, vascular and functional neurosurgery, together with the fundamentals of spinal surgery and peri-operative complication management.

The emphasis throughout is on sound operative reasoning rather than technique in isolation.

discussions.name: Dr. P. Ahmadi
discussions.body: How do you approach localizing a lesion clinically, before any imaging?

discussions.name: Dr. N. Farahani
discussions.body: Separate central from peripheral first, then work by level — cortex, subcortex, brainstem, cord, root, nerve, junction, muscle. The pattern of weakness, the reflexes and any sensory level usually narrow it to one or two sites before you order a single test.

discussions.name: S. Rahimi
discussions.body: Which examination findings carry the most localizing value?

discussions.name: Dr. N. Farahani
discussions.body: Reflex asymmetry, a discrete sensory level, and the distribution of weakness are highest-yield. Pronator drift and observed gait are remarkably sensitive screens when time is short.

discussions.name: Dr. M. Kazemi
discussions.body: Any practical rule for separating migraine from a secondary headache in clinic?

discussions.name: Dr. L. Hosseini
discussions.body: Run the red-flag screen first — thunderclap onset, new headache over 50, immunosuppression, focal signs or papilloedema. A stereotyped pattern over years with a normal examination is reassuringly primary.

discussions.name: A. Tehrani
discussions.body: Could you add a worked case on the first unprovoked seizure?

discussions.name: M. Davari
discussions.body: How does neuroplasticity actually affect learning?

discussions.name: Dr. S. Moradi
discussions.body: Learning is largely synaptic remodelling — long-term potentiation strengthens active synapses while unused connections weaken. Repetition and salience decide which circuits are consolidated, which is why spaced, meaningful practice works.

discussions.name: Dr. R. Najafi
discussions.body: Which neurotransmitters are most important clinically?

discussions.name: Dr. S. Moradi
discussions.body: Dopamine, acetylcholine, GABA, glutamate and serotonin between them underlie most of what we prescribe — from antiparkinsonian and anticholinesterase drugs to antiepileptics and antidepressants.

discussions.name: N. Eskandari
discussions.body: Is the resting membrane potential maintained mainly by the Na/K pump?

discussions.name: Dr. H. Bagheri
discussions.body: The pump establishes the ionic gradients, but the resting potential is set chiefly by the membrane’s resting permeability to potassium. The pump’s direct electrogenic contribution is small.

discussions.name: Dr. K. Sadeghi
discussions.body: What imaging sequence is most useful for acute stroke?

discussions.name: Dr. A. Karimi
discussions.body: DWI remains the most sensitive sequence during the hyperacute phase — restricted diffusion appears within minutes, well before changes are visible on CT or conventional MRI.

discussions.name: F. Mousavi
discussions.body: When should I choose CT over MRI in the emergency department?

discussions.name: Dr. A. Karimi
discussions.body: CT first for suspected acute haemorrhage, trauma, or an unstable patient — it is fast and highly sensitive to fresh blood. Reach for MRI when you need tissue characterisation or posterior-fossa detail.

discussions.name: Dr. T. Jalali
discussions.body: Any common pitfall when reading DWI?

discussions.name: Dr. Z. Rostami
discussions.body: T2 shine-through is the classic trap — always confirm true restriction on the ADC map before calling acute ischaemia.

discussions.name: B. Ghorbani
discussions.body: Which structures do you find most difficult to identify on cross-section?

discussions.name: Dr. R. Tabrizi
discussions.body: The thalamic nuclei and the brainstem tracts trip up most learners. Fix the major landmarks first, then reason inward — relative position is far more reliable than trying to memorise every nucleus in isolation.

discussions.name: Dr. S. Amiri
discussions.body: What anatomy is most relevant clinically, day to day?

discussions.name: Dr. R. Tabrizi
discussions.body: The internal capsule, the brainstem cranial-nerve nuclei, and the arterial territories. Together they account for the majority of localisable deficits you will meet on the ward.

discussions.name: M. Khalili
discussions.body: Is it worth learning the cerebellar peduncles in detail?

discussions.name: Dr. P. Ranjbar
discussions.body: Yes — knowing which peduncle carries what makes cerebellar and brainstem syndromes much easier to reason through.

discussions.name: Dr. A. Shirazi
discussions.body: What is your first-line strategy for an acute rise in ICP?

discussions.name: Dr. L. Hashemi
discussions.body: Optimise the basics first — head up 30°, neck neutral, normocapnia, adequate sedation and analgesia — then escalate to osmotherapy. Hyperosmolar therapy buys time; it never replaces treating the underlying cause.

discussions.name: Dr. N. Yazdani
discussions.body: Hypertonic saline or mannitol for raised ICP?

discussions.name: Dr. L. Hashemi
discussions.body: Either lowers ICP; let volume status decide. Mannitol if euvolaemic with good renal function; hypertonic saline if hypovolaemic or hyponatraemic. Track the osmolar gap and sodium closely either way.

discussions.name: Dr. H. Mahmoudi
discussions.body: What do you find hardest about running the neuro-ICU?

discussions.name: Dr. F. Sadr
discussions.body: Balancing competing targets — perfusion against oedema, sedation against preserving the neurological examination. Multimodal monitoring helps, but clinical judgement still makes the call.

discussions.name: Dr. O. Mirzaei
discussions.body: What is the real role of neuronavigation in routine cases?

discussions.name: Dr. M. Saadat
discussions.body: It is most valuable for planning the trajectory and craniotomy, and for deep or small lesions. Stay aware of brain shift after the dura is opened — re-orient to fixed landmarks and do not trust it blindly late in the case.

discussions.name: D. Akbari
discussions.body: What goes into surgical planning before a tumour resection?

discussions.name: Dr. M. Saadat
discussions.body: Define the lesion and its relationship to eloquent cortex and vessels on MRI, choose the approach and positioning, and settle the adjuncts — navigation, monitoring, awake mapping — before the patient is anaesthetised.

discussions.name: Dr. S. Lotfi
discussions.body: When do you add intra-operative neuromonitoring?

discussions.name: Dr. M. Saadat
discussions.body: Whenever the approach puts motor, brainstem or cranial-nerve pathways at risk. The trend across the case is more informative than any single reading.

pastDetail.overview: This session brought together over sixty clinicians from neurology, neurophysiology, emergency medicine, and intensive care for a structured day of expert-led presentations and case-based workshops. The programme centred on the practical management of complex neurological emergencies, with particular attention to the evidence base for current treatment protocols and the clinical situations where that evidence is absent or contested. Speakers were drawn from tertiary referral centres across the region, and the case discussions reflected the genuine diagnostic uncertainty that characterises daily practice at the interface of neurology and critical care. Participants rated the session highly for relevance, and several of the clinical frameworks introduced during the workshops have since been integrated into institutional protocols by attending teams.

reservation.eventDesc:
This focused half-day programme brings together neurologists, neurophysiologists, and allied clinical teams for a series of expert-led presentations built around real case material, with time reserved after each talk for questions from the floor.

The morning addresses the acute assessment of the neurologically deteriorating patient — new-onset seizures in the emergency setting, the management of status epilepticus, and a practical framework for evaluating encephalopathy. The afternoon turns to procedural topics: EEG monitoring in the ICU and a workshop-style review of challenging traces.

All registered attendees receive a pre-reading pack, a printed programme on the day, and access to the session slide deck within 72 hours. Certificates of attendance are issued automatically, and seats are limited, so early registration is strongly recommended.

people.name: Prof. Ali Shalash
people.title: Professor of Clinical Neurology
people.bio: Prof. Ali Shalash is an Iranian Persian doctor and professor of clinical neurology whose teaching anchors the Academy’s Clinical Neurology course. His work centres on the neurological examination, lesion localisation and movement disorders, taught in a methodical, bedside-first style. Drawing on years of clinical practice and academic teaching, he guides learners from the history and examination through to a prioritised differential diagnosis.
people.methodology: Prof. Shalash teaches in a structured, case-led way: each topic begins as a clinical problem at the bedside, is worked through from presentation to localisation and management, and is reinforced with the high-yield reasoning expected of postgraduate trainees. The sequence is deliberately cumulative, building toward independent diagnostic judgement.
people.impact: His clinical neurology teaching supports residents and students preparing for practice and board assessment, and provides the Academy’s Clinical Neurology course with a coherent pathway from the bedside examination to a confident differential diagnosis.

people.name: Dr. Sam Webster
people.title: Anatomist & Neuroscience Educator
people.bio: Sam Webster is an anatomist and neuroscience educator whose clear, structured teaching of the human brain underpins the Academy’s Brain Anatomy course. He is known for making complex neuroanatomy approachable — moving through surface landmarks, the brainstem, the deep grey matter and the white-matter pathways in a logical, region-by-region sequence that always ties structure back to clinical function.
people.methodology: Sam Webster teaches with a calm, narrative style: each structure is introduced in context, oriented against fixed landmarks, and immediately related to the deficit it produces when damaged. Three-dimensional relationships are built up step by step rather than memorised in isolation, which suits learners moving from first exposure toward confident localisation.
people.impact: His anatomy teaching has reached students of medicine and the allied health sciences, and within the Academy it forms the visual backbone of the Brain Anatomy course — giving clinicians a durable, examination-ready mental model of cerebral structure.

about.pullquote: — a heritage of precision, a future of partnership —

story.title: Built on engineering, drawn by care
story.body: Founded by biomedical engineers with deep clinical experience, Neuro Tech began as a specialised neurology importer and has grown, slowly and deliberately, into a global supplier, academy and agency partner — present in research institutes, hospitals and clinics across four continents.

mission.title: Mission
mission.desc: To render best-in-class neurology equipment and education accessible to clinicians worldwide, through dependable sourcing and uncompromised service.

vision.title: Vision
vision.desc: A global standard of neurological care, supported by considered partnerships between manufacturers, distributors, educators and clinicians.

timeline.event: Founded as a biomedical engineering practice.
Granted national import licence for neurology devices.
First exclusive agency partnership with a European manufacturer.
Expanded into export markets across the Middle East.
Partner network reaches ten countries and one hundred institutions.
Launch of Neuro Tech Academy and the global events programme.

items.title: Precision
items.desc: Every device, document and lesson is held to a clinical standard. Nothing ships, prints or publishes until it is exact.

items.title: Partnership
items.desc: We grow through long, exclusive relationships rather than transactions — with manufacturers, clinicians and educators alike.

items.title: Pedagogy
items.desc: Knowledge is the product. Our academy turns equipment expertise into teachable, examinable clinical skill.

collaborate.title: Collaborate with us
collaborate.desc: Whether you manufacture neurology equipment, lead a clinical department, or teach the next generation of specialists — there is a place for considered partnership here.

items.title: Manufacturers
items.desc: Exclusive distribution and full regulatory representation across our territories.

items.title: Institutions
